Financial and Estate Planning Literacy: Item Validation and Categorical CFA

Author

Jamie C. Lee

Published

August 6, 2026

Summary

This document implements the analyses set out in the project’s written analysis plan (Financial and EP Literacy Pre-registration.docx) on ep_literacy_data_08.04.xlsx (N = 399 participants recruited on Prolific).

ImportantThe analysis plan was not filed with a registry

That document is an internal plan written before the analyses were run. It was never submitted to AsPredicted, OSF, or any other registry, so nothing here is pre-registered in the sense that word carries in a paper, and none of it should be described that way. Where this document distinguishes planned analyses from post hoc ones, that distinction reflects the order in which decisions were actually made – it is a statement about this project’s history, not a claim anyone else can verify.

The document proceeds in six parts:

  1. Bot exclusion checks, using the prompt-injection fake-item question (fake_gg) and the reverse-shibboleth apple-juice nutrition questions (mr_*), plus an exploratory look at whether the top of the score distribution shows signs of outside help. This comes first because it defines the post-exclusion sample that every later section reports alongside the full one.
  2. Measures and scoring: the item set, the factor assignment, and the scoring rules.
  3. Descriptives for the 12 financial literacy (FL) items and the 12 estate planning literacy (EPL) items – pass rates, “I don’t know” rates, total-score distributions, item-rest correlations, a distractor analysis, and the planned item flags.
  4. Categorical CFAs comparing the planned one-, two-, and three-factor models, fit to the full sample and re-fit to the post-exclusion sample as a consistency check.
  5. Factor-structure analysis (exploratory) testing the three-factor model against all the ways the three item blocks could be merged, whether FL sits closer to one EPL dimension than the other, and the hierarchical alternatives.
  6. Summary of both hypotheses across the full and post-exclusion samples, with the caveats that belong in a write-up.

Section 1 refers to scores that are defined in Section 2; the scoring rules are simply “blank = incorrect, option 1 = correct except for fin_13,” and the full statement is in Section 3.2.

Headline result. In the full sample, the two-factor model fits significantly better than the one-factor model (scaled \(\Delta\chi^2\)(1) = 37.76, p < .001), and the three-factor model fits significantly better than the two-factor model (scaled \(\Delta\chi^2\)(2) = 22.16, p < .001). Both H1 and H2 are supported on the model-comparison leg of the decision rule, and the two- and three-factor models both clear conventional absolute fit thresholds. The same pattern holds after bot exclusions.

Three constructs, not two. The exploratory analysis in Section 7 tests the three-factor model against every possible two-factor merge, not just the planned one. It wins each time. The financial-consequences EPL block sits between financial literacy and legal/administrative EPL – somewhat closer to FL, but the difference between those two correlations is borderline (p ≈ .05) and should not be reported as established.

But a general factor dominates. Section 7.5 fits the hierarchical alternatives. A second-order model is algebraically identical to the three-factor model here and adds nothing. A bifactor model does add something, and what it shows is that roughly 69% of the common variance across the 24 items belongs to a single general knowledge factor; the EPL-financial specific factor disappears altogether. The three dimensions are separable, but they are separable facets of a dominant common ability, and the subscale-level reliabilities (ωHS ≈ .29) are too low to interpret FL or EPL-Legal subscores on their own.

NoteTwo items needed decisions before any model was fit

fin_13 is keyed to response option 4, not option 1. The distractor analysis in Section 4.6 flagged option 1 as behaving like a wrong answer (pass rate 4.0%, item-rest r = –.20, and a negative loading on the FL factor), while option 4 behaved like the correct one (r = +.38). This matches the substance of the item: at a 12% APR the interest on $3,000 is exactly the $30 monthly payment, so the debt is never eliminated. The key was corrected and confirmed.

fin_8 is dropped from this document entirely – from the descriptives as well as the models. The item asked whether withdrawals from a 401(k)/IRA are required after age 70½. Under every candidate key it failed to discriminate: keying 2 as correct gave an item-rest correlation of +.01 and a standardized FL loading of .02; keying 2 or 3 gave +.03 and .03; even the original 1-key reached only +.12, against a .25–.49 range for every other FL item. No response option separated high scorers from low scorers, so re-keying could not rescue it. Fitting the models with fin_8 retained (under either key) left every conclusion unchanged and fit marginally worse. All counts in this document are therefore out of 12 FL items and 12 EPL items, 24 in total.

1 Bot Exclusion Checks

The analysis plan named two behavioral bot indicators, both adapted from Zhang et al. Neither the keystroke/paste telemetry variables (StrokeCount_AI, PasteFlag_AI, etc.) nor survey duration are used for exclusion here, per your instruction.

1.1 Prompt-Injection Fake Item

Participants saw a list of apple juice brands and were asked to select the ones they buy regularly. Embedded in the option text was an instruction directed at an automated agent, telling it to choose “Golden Grove” – a brand that does not exist. A human reading the question for its face content has no reason to select it. fake_gg = 1 records that selection.

Did not select 384 96.2

1.2 Reverse-Shibboleth Nutrition Items

Participants estimated the calories, carbohydrates, fat, and protein in an 8 oz. glass of apple juice, without looking anything up. The “superhuman knowledge” criterion requires all four estimates to land in the true bands: 105–120 calories, 26–29 g carbohydrates, 0–0.5 g fat, and 0–1 g protein.

Table 2. Reverse-Shibboleth Items: Accuracy by Component
Component N in band % in band
Calories (105-120) 60 15.0
Carbohydrates (26-29 g) 22 5.5
Fat (0-0.5 g) 217 54.4
Protein (0-1 g) 238 59.6
Table 3. Number of Nutrition Estimates Falling in the Correct Band
Components in band (of 4) N %
0 117 29.3
1 89 22.3
2 146 36.6
3 32 8.0
4 15 3.8
Only participants with all 4 in band are flagged.

The fat and protein bands are easy to hit by accident because both true values are near zero and “0” is a common lay guess (54.4% and 59.6% of participants land in band on those two alone). The calories and carbohydrate bands are the discriminating ones, and requiring all four simultaneously is what makes the rule specific.

1.5 Score Distributions and Possible External Assistance

Neither criterion targets participants who simply looked answers up. A participant using a search engine or a chatbot on the knowledge items would not necessarily select the fake apple juice brand or produce textbook-accurate nutrition figures, but would leave a different trace: a near-perfect score, no blanks, and – because looking things up takes time – a longer rather than shorter survey duration. This section reports the score distributions with that question in mind. Nothing here is used for exclusion; it is diagnostic only, and no analysis in this document conditions on it.

Every table in this section reports the full sample and the post-exclusion sample side by side, so it is always visible how much of any anomaly the bot rules already remove.

In the full sample, 66 participants (16.5%) answered all 12 FL items correctly and 31 (7.8%) answered all 12 EPL items correctly.

Note the shape difference. The FL distribution is smoothly left-skewed with its mode at 10–11, and the perfect-score bar is smaller than the bars adjacent to it – the normal ceiling pattern. The EPL distribution is not smooth: the count at 12 (31) is nearly double the count at 11 (16), which no ordinary ability distribution produces.

The bot exclusions remove most of that spike. Post-exclusion, EPL = 12 falls from 31 to 17 while EPL = 11 barely moves (16 to 14), so the ratio between them drops from 1.94 to 1.21. Of the 27 excluded participants, 14 – 52% of them – had a perfect EPL score, against a base rate of 7.8% in the sample as a whole. The exclusion rule was built with no knowledge of the quiz responses, yet it lands squarely on the anomaly.

The spike does not disappear entirely: EPL = 12 (17) still exceeds EPL = 11 (14) after exclusions. Some residual excess remains at the ceiling.

The joint table concentrates the pattern. 24 participants answered every one of the 24 items correctly. If perfect FL and perfect EPL scores were independent you would expect 5.1.

The cell is also out of line with its own neighbours. Missing one FL item while acing EPL occurs 3 time(s), and missing one EPL item while acing FL occurs 4 time(s) – both far below the 24 who missed nothing at all. Ability distributions do not produce a peak at the boundary with troughs immediately beside it; they taper into it.

After exclusions the knot loosens but does not untie: perfect-on-both falls from 24 to 13, and the wider top-right corner (missing at most one item on each scale) from 39 to 25.

1.5.4 Overlap With the Bot Detectors

The score bands and the bot flags are measured independently – nothing in the exclusion rule looks at a knowledge item. If the top of the score distribution were simply the high-ability tail, flag rates should be flat across bands.

Table 12. Do High Scorers Trip the Bot Detectors? (Fisher's Exact Tests)
Detector Flagged among top band Flagged among rest Odds ratio 95% CI p
Golden Grove (prompt injection) 4 / 31 (12.9%) 11 / 368 (3.0%) 4.8 [1.0, 17.6] 0.022
Reverse shibboleth (all 4 in band) 11 / 31 (35.5%) 4 / 368 (1.1%) 48.5 [13.0, 226.8] < .001
Either criterion 13 / 31 (41.9%) 14 / 368 (3.8%) 17.9 [6.7, 48.5] < .001
Each row compares participants in the top score band against everyone else. Odds ratios are conditional MLEs from Fisher's exact test.

They are not flat. The flag rate is between 1.2% and 7.9% in the bottom four bands and jumps to 41.9% in the top band – an odds ratio of 17.9 (p < .001) for being flagged if you scored 23+.

But the two detectors do not contribute equally. The reverse-shibboleth criterion carries essentially all of the signal: 11 of the 31 top scorers trip it (OR = 48.5, p < .001), against only 4 who select Golden Grove (OR = 4.8, p = 0.022, resting on 4 participants).

That asymmetry is worth pausing on, because it cuts both ways:

  • It is substantively coherent. The shibboleth detects implausibly precise factual recall; looking up estate planning answers and looking up apple juice nutrition are the same behaviour applied to different questions. The prompt-injection item detects something narrower – an agent that reads and obeys embedded instructions – which a human using ChatGPT in a separate tab would never trigger.
  • It also means the convergence is weaker evidence than two fully independent detectors agreeing. Both the shibboleth and the quiz score are accuracy measures. They are about unrelated content, so this is not circular, but a single detector carrying the result is a thinner reed than the “two independent indicators converge” framing would suggest.

What the exclusions do to the anomaly. The exclusion rule removes 27 participants, of whom 13 scored 23+ – 48% of all exclusions come from the top 8% of the score distribution. The 23+ group shrinks from 31 to 18 and perfect 25/25 scores from 24 to 0. The ceiling excess is substantially reduced, though as noted above it is not fully eliminated.

What the diagnostics show.

  • High scorers took longer, not less time (median 24.8 min in the 23-24 band vs. 18.1 min in the 10-13 band). This rules out fast random-clicking but is exactly what looking answers up would produce. It also means a duration-based exclusion rule would fail to catch them.
  • High scorers left essentially nothing blank (mean 0.0 items vs. 3.3 in the 10-13 band). This is partly mechanical – a blank is scored wrong, so a high scorer cannot have many – and so is weak evidence on its own.

How to read this. None of it identifies any individual participant as having used outside help. A genuinely knowledgeable respondent – an estate attorney, a financial planner – produces the same row in the table above, and 18 of the 31 top scorers trip no detector at all. What the evidence supports is narrower: the upper tail contains more participants than an ability distribution alone would generate, and that excess overlaps heavily with the participants the bot criteria already remove.

Adding a performance-based exclusion now would mean building a rule around the outcome variable after seeing it, which is the kind of choice that inflates whatever result follows. Because the plan was never registered, there is no external record that the current rule came first – a reason to be more conservative about changing it, not less. My recommendation is to leave the exclusion rule as written, report this section as an exploratory data-quality observation, and address it at the design stage in the next wave (an item pool that resists lookup, or per-item timing captured for the knowledge block). If you do want a sensitivity analysis, the defensible version is to refit the models dropping the 24 perfect scorers and report it explicitly as post hoc – say the word and I will add it.

Participants who have received an inheritance score meaningfully higher on both scales, and the gap is larger for estate planning literacy (d = 0.52) than for financial literacy (d = 0.36). Term Estimate SE t p

Age (years) 0.025 0.010 2.59 0.010

WarningAge is a serious confound here

Participants who have received an inheritance are on average 11.8 years older (54.0 vs. 42.1). Inheriting is largely a function of how long you have lived and whether your parents have died, so any raw comparison of inheritors to non-inheritors is partly an age comparison.

Adjusting for age shrinks the effect but does not remove it: inheritance is still worth +1.20 points of estate planning literacy (p < .001) with age held constant. Treat this as a descriptive association worth following up, not as evidence that inheriting causes literacy – both could follow from family circumstances this survey does not measure, such as whether the family had assets worth planning around in the first place.

3 Measures and Scoring

3.1 Items and Hypothesized Factor Assignment

The analysis plan specified 13 FL items (from Fernandes et al., 2014), 3 EPL items covering financial consequences, and 9 EPL items covering legal/administrative consequences. One FL item (fin_8) is dropped for non-discrimination, leaving 12. Assignment of the 12 ep_* items to the two EPL subscales follows item content: ep_1–ep_9 concern what a legal instrument does or who has legal authority (intestacy, beneficiary designations, right of survivorship, powers of attorney, trust funding, guardianship), whereas ep_10–ep_12 concern the monetary consequences of an estate’s composition (debt satisfaction, illiquidity, net vs. gross value).

3.2 Scoring Rules

All 24 knowledge items are scored as binary correct/incorrect:

  • Response option 1 = correct for every item except fin_13, where 4 = correct (“you would never eliminate the debt”). That key was identified by the distractor analysis in Section 4.6 and confirmed against the instrument.
  • A blank response = “I don’t know”, which is scored as incorrect, not as missing data. Every participant therefore contributes a complete response vector, and the CFAs are estimated on complete data with no listwise deletion or FIML.

Because every indicator is binary, all models declare the items as ordered and use the WLSMV estimator (diagonally weighted least squares with mean- and variance-adjusted test statistics), as planned.

4.4 Item-Rest Correlations

Each item’s corrected item-rest correlation is the point-biserial correlation between that item (0/1) and the sum of the other items on its own hypothesized scale. A negative value means participants who score well on the rest of the scale tend to get that item wrong – a standard indicator of a miskeyed, confusing, or off-construct item.

4.5 Tetrachoric Correlation Structure

Tetrachoric correlations estimate the correlation between the continuous latent propensities underlying two binary responses, and are the appropriate input for factor-analyzing binary items. If FL and EPL are distinguishable, the FL block and the EPL block should each cohere more tightly internally than they do with each other.

Diagonal = mean within-block correlation; off-diagonal = mean cross-block correlation.

4.6 Response-Option Key Check

To distinguish “hard item” from “miskeyed item,” this section performs a distractor analysis. For each response option of each item, it builds a 0/1 indicator (“did this participant choose this option?”) and correlates it with the participant’s summed score on the other items of the same scale — the item itself is excluded, so an item cannot be correlated with a total that already contains it. Blank responses count as “did not choose this option.”

The logic: participants who do well on the rest of the scale should be the ones picking the correct answer, so the correct option should have the highest and most positive correlation, and the distractors should be negative. If the keyed option is not the best-behaving option, the key is suspect.

These are correlations, not score differences. A correlation of .49 on a 12-item scale corresponds to about a 2.2-point gap in rest-score between those who chose the option and those who did not; a correlation of .03 corresponds to about 0.2 points, which is nothing. The translation is $ ext{mean difference} = r imes SD_{ ext{rest}} / $, where \(p\) is the share choosing the option — so the same correlation implies a bigger raw gap for rarely chosen options than for common ones.

This check is what identified the original fin_13 keying error. Under the initial “1 = correct” key, fin_13 passed at 4.0% with an item-rest correlation of –.20 and a standardized FL loading of –.57, while option 4 showed r = +.38. The key was corrected to 4 and the item now behaves normally; the table below reflects the corrected key.

5 Categorical CFA: Full Sample

5.1 Model Specification

All three models are estimated with WLSMV on the binary scored items, with delta parameterization and theta/threshold defaults as implemented in lavaan::cfa(ordered = ...). Latent variables are identified by fixing the first loading to 1 and standardized loadings are reported from standardizedSolution().

  • One-factor: a single general knowledge factor G with all 24 items as indicators.
  • Two-factor: FL (13 fin_* items) and EPL (all 12 ep_* items), freely correlated.
  • Three-factor: FL, EPL_FIN (ep_10–ep_12), and EPL_LEG (ep_1–ep_9), all freely correlated.

7 Which Factor Structure Do the Data Support?

ImportantThis section is exploratory

The analysis plan named exactly three models – one-factor, two-factor (FL vs. undifferentiated EPL), and three-factor – and the nested comparisons among them. Those are reported in Sections 5 and 6.

Everything in this section was decided after looking at the data. The alternative two-factor groupings, the test of whether FL sits closer to one EPL dimension than the other, and the hierarchical models below were not part of the plan. They are legitimate exploratory measurement work, but they must be labelled exploratory in any write-up, and their p-values should not be presented as confirmatory. Because the plan was never registered, the planned/exploratory line here rests on the project’s own records rather than on a timestamped filing.

7.1 The Five Possible Groupings

The three item blocks – FL (12 items), EPL-Fin (3 items), and EPL-Legal (9 items) – can be organised into latent factors on a single level in exactly five ways. (Hierarchical structures, where a general factor sits above or behind the three, are a separate family and are handled in Section 7.5.)

Label Structure Substantive reading
1F {FL + EPL-Fin + EPL-Legal} One undifferentiated knowledge ability
2F-A {FL} {EPL-Fin + EPL-Legal} Pre-registered: financial literacy vs. estate planning literacy
2F-B {FL + EPL-Fin} {EPL-Legal} Money knowledge vs. legal/procedural knowledge
2F-C {FL + EPL-Legal} {EPL-Fin} EPL-Fin as the outlier block
3F {FL} {EPL-Fin} {EPL-Legal} Three separable abilities

Every two-factor model is nested inside the three-factor model: merging two factors is equivalent to fixing their correlation to 1, which (because a correlation matrix with \(r_{23} = 1\) forces \(r_{12} = r_{13}\)) costs 2 degrees of freedom. Each can therefore be tested against 3F with a scaled difference test. The three two-factor models have identical degrees of freedom, so although they are not nested in one another, their fit indices are directly comparable.

7.2 Fit of the Five Models

7.3 Nested Tests Against the Three-Factor Model

Table 50. Each Simpler Grouping Tested Against the Three-Factor Model
Sample Restricted model Scaled chi2 diff df diff p 3F preferred
Full 1F 64.62 3 < .001 yes
2F-A 22.16 2 < .001 yes
2F-B 20.84 2 < .001 yes
2F-C 72.90 2 < .001 yes
Post-exclusion 1F 59.21 3 < .001 yes
2F-A 20.67 2 < .001 yes
2F-B 20.39 2 < .001 yes
2F-C 62.93 2 < .001 yes
A significant result means the simpler model fits significantly worse, i.e. the three-factor model is preferred.

Two or three? Three. Every simpler grouping fits significantly worse than the three-factor model, in both samples, with no comparison close to the .05 boundary. It also has the best absolute fit of the five in both samples (CFI = 0.965 full, 0.966 post-exclusion) and the lowest WRMR; in the full sample it is the only grouping with WRMR below the conventional 1.0 cutoff for categorical data (0.959, against 1.024 for 2F-A and 1.010 for 2F-B).

Which two-factor grouping is best, if you were forced to pick two? 2F-B. The three two-factor models have identical degrees of freedom (251), so their chi-squares are directly comparable: 2F-B (\(\chi^2\) = 359.1) edges out the plan-specified 2F-A (\(\chi^2\) = 366.3), while 2F-C (\(\chi^2\) = 428.5) is far worse. So if the EPL-Fin block has to be attached to something, it attaches marginally better to FL than to EPL-Legal – but the gap between 2F-B and 2F-A is 7.2 chi-square points on equal df, which is not a difference worth building an argument on. What the data say clearly is that neither merge should be made.

The decisive comparison is 2F-C: forcing EPL-Fin to stand alone against everything else costs 72.9 chi-square points. EPL-Fin is not a free-floating block; it is genuinely intermediate between the other two.

7.4 Is FL Closer to EPL-Fin than to EPL-Legal?

In the three-factor model the two correlations involving FL are not equal by inspection. Testing whether the difference is reliable requires comparing two dependent correlations estimated from the same model, which is done here two ways: a delta-method Wald test on the difference as a derived parameter, and a scaled likelihood-ratio test against a model that constrains the two correlations to be equal.

Table 51. Testing r(FL, EPL-Fin) = r(FL, EPL-Legal) in the Three-Factor Model
Sample r(FL, EPL-Fin) r(FL, EPL-Legal) Difference SE 95% CI Wald z Wald p LRT chi2(1) LRT p
Full 0.794 0.673 0.120 0.062 [-0.000, 0.241] 1.95 0.051 3.78 0.052
Post-exclusion 0.771 0.631 0.141 0.070 [0.004, 0.277] 2.02 0.043 4.01 0.045
Estimated with std.lv = TRUE so the latent covariances are correlations. Wald test = delta-method test on the derived difference; LRT = scaled difference test against a model constraining the two correlations equal.

Directionally yes, statistically borderline. FL correlates more strongly with EPL-Fin than with EPL-Legal in both samples, by about 0.12 to 0.14 correlation points. But the test sits astride the conventional threshold: p = 0.052 in the full sample and p = 0.045 post-exclusion. A result that lands on 0.052 and 0.045 in two overlapping samples is one that changes its verdict depending on which sample you happen to report, which is exactly the situation where the honest summary is “suggestive, underpowered, not established.”

The EPL_FIN factor rests on only three indicators, so its correlations are estimated with wide intervals (Figure 20) that overlap substantially. Nothing here is strong enough to support a claim in a paper that FL is more related to the financial dimension of estate planning knowledge than to the legal one. It is a good hypothesis for the next study, powered for it.

7.5 Hierarchical Alternatives: Second-Order and Bifactor

All five groupings above put the factors on the same level – they disagree only about how many boxes the items go in. A different family of models asks a different question: is there a general ability sitting above or behind the specific ones?

Model Structure What it claims
Second-order Items → 3 first-order factors → 1 general factor The three factors are correlated because they are all indicators of one broader ability
Bifactor Items → 1 general factor and → 3 specific factors, all orthogonal Every item reflects a general ability plus a domain-specific residual; the two are separated, not layered

The distinction matters. In a second-order model the general factor explains the items only through the first-order factors. In a bifactor model the general factor loads on every item directly, and each specific factor captures only what is left over within its own block after the general factor is accounted for. That second structure is what lets you ask how much of each item is general versus domain-specific – a question the correlated-factors model cannot answer.

7.5.1 The Second-Order Model Is the Three-Factor Model

With three first-order factors, the second-order level is just-identified: three second-order loadings and three disturbances reproduce the three factor variances and three covariances exactly, with nothing left over to constrain. The second-order model is therefore a reparameterization of the correlated three-factor model, not a competing hypothesis, and it cannot be tested against it.

Table 52. Second-Order vs. Correlated Three-Factor: Identical by Construction
Model chi2 df npar CFI TLI RMSEA WRMR
Correlated three-factor 332.0 249 51 0.965 0.961 0.029 0.959
Second-order (GEN above the three) 332.0 249 51 0.965 0.961 0.029 0.959
Identical chi-square, df, and number of free parameters. The two models are algebraically equivalent, so no difference test is possible or meaningful.

It is still worth reading the second-order loadings, because they say which block is the purest marker of whatever general ability the three share.

Table 53. Second-Order Loadings (Full Sample)
Second-order factor First-order factor Std. loading SE 95% CI
GEN FL 0.840 0.043 [0.756, 0.924]
GEN EPL_FIN 0.945 0.046 [0.854, 1.035]
GEN EPL_LEG 0.802 0.048 [0.707, 0.896]

EPL_FIN loads on the general factor at 0.945 – higher than FL or EPL_LEG. The financial-consequence block is the closest thing in the battery to a pure measure of general knowledge, which is the same fact that made it sit between the other two blocks in Section 7.4.

7.5.2 The Bifactor Model Does Not Hold Together

Fitting the full bifactor – a general factor plus all three specific factors – fails.

Table 54. Degenerate Estimates in the Full Bifactor Model
Parameter Estimate
EPF_S =~ ep_10 0.000
EPF_S =~ ep_11 0.001
EPF_S =~ ep_12 97.930
Residual variance of ep_12 -9589.8
lavaan additionally reports that the information matrix could not be inverted, so no standard errors or robust fit statistics are available for this model.

Two of the three EPL_FIN specific loadings are pinned at zero, the third runs away to 98, and ep_12 is handed a residual variance of -9590 to compensate. This is empirical under-identification, and it is not a nuisance to be worked around – it is the result. Once a general factor is allowed to explain the items directly, the three financial-consequence items have essentially no shared variance left over. There is no residual “financial-consequence” dimension for a specific factor to capture.

Two principled repairs both say the same thing.

Constraining the three EPL_FIN specific loadings to a single common value makes the model estimable and turns “is there residual specificity here?” into a one-parameter test. The answer is barely: the common loading is 0.236 in the full sample (p = 0.023) and 0.229 post-exclusion (p = 0.058, CI includes zero). Dropping the factor entirely costs almost nothing in fit. The rest of this section uses that reduced model – a general factor, an FL specific factor, and an EPL-Legal specific factor, with the three EPL-Fin items loading on the general factor only – because it is the one that estimates cleanly, with all residual variances positive (minimum = 0.374).

A dominant general factor. 69% of the common variance across the 24 items belongs to the general factor, and 85% of the reliable variance in a 24-item total score is general-factor variance (ωH = 0.790 against ω = 0.929). By the benchmarks in the bifactor literature – ECV > .60, PUC > .70, ωH > .70 as indicators that multidimensionality is not severe enough to distort a total score – these data sit on the “essentially unidimensional enough to score as a total” side on two of three criteria, with PUC (0.630) just below.

The subscales carry little unique reliable variance. ωHS is 0.290 for the FL specific factor and 0.287 for EPL-Legal. Both are far below the ~.50 that is usually treated as the minimum for interpreting a subscale score on its own. Once you remove what the items share with everything else, an FL subscore or an EPL-Legal subscore is mostly noise.

But the specific factors are not nothing. 5 of 24 items have I-ECV below .50, meaning most of their common variance is domain-specific rather than general. ep_7 (retirement account beneficiary vs. will) is the extreme case at I-ECV = 0.271, and fin_1, fin_2, and fin_5 are similarly specific-heavy. There is real domain structure here; it is just outweighed by the general factor.

7.5.4 Reconciling This With the Three-Factor Result

These findings are not in conflict, but they are easy to report as if they were.

  • Section 7 asked “are the three blocks distinguishable?” The answer is yes: forcing any two of them to correlate at 1.0 fits significantly worse.
  • This section asks “how much of the item variance is shared across all three?” The answer is most of it.

A construct can be statistically separable and still contribute little unique reliable variance to a score. Both statements are true of these data, and a write-up that reports only the first would overstate what the EPL subscales do.

The bifactor also explains why EPL_FIN behaved the way it did earlier. Its three items have the highest general-factor loadings in the whole battery (0.62, 0.75, 0.78) and no residual specificity at all. That is exactly the profile that makes a block appear to sit between two others in a correlated-factors solution, and it is why the FL–EPL-Fin correlation was the highest of the three: both are being pulled by the same general ability, with EPL-Fin contributing almost nothing else.

WarningCaveats on the bifactor result
  • The bifactor model is not nested within the correlated three-factor model, so the fit comparison in Table 55 is descriptive. Bifactor models are also known to fit better than their competitors almost as a rule, because the extra orthogonal factors absorb residual covariance regardless of whether a general factor is substantively real.
  • The model reported here is a reduced bifactor with one specific factor deleted after seeing that the full version failed. That is a data-driven simplification and belongs in the exploratory bucket with everything else in this section.
  • Bifactor indices computed from binary items under WLSMV are less well studied than their continuous-data counterparts. Treat the exact values as approximate.

7.6 Verdict

Table 59. Answers to the Structural Questions (Exploratory)
Question Answer Evidence
Two constructs or three? Three 3F beats all four simpler groupings, both samples (all p < .001). 3F has the best CFI (0.965 full, 0.966 post-exclusion) and lowest WRMR of the five.
Is r(FL, EPL-Fin) > r(FL, EPL-Legal)? Directionally yes; borderline Difference = 0.120 (full) / 0.141 (post-exclusion); LRT p = 0.052 / 0.045. Straddles .05.
Should FL and EPL-Fin be merged into one construct? No 2F-B fits significantly worse than 3F (chi2(2) = 20.8, p < .001).
Should EPL-Fin and EPL-Legal be merged (the planned 2-factor model)? No 2F-A fits significantly worse than 3F (chi2(2) = 22.2, p < .001).
Is a general factor behind all three? Yes, and it dominates Bifactor: ECV = 0.691, omega-H/omega = 0.850. The EPL-Fin specific factor vanishes entirely.
Do the subscales carry usable unique variance? Barely omega-HS = 0.290 (FL) and 0.287 (EPL-Legal), both well below the ~.50 needed to interpret a subscore.

The picture is a three-factor structure sitting on top of a strong general factor. The three blocks are genuinely separable – every merge fits significantly worse – but most of what the items measure is shared across all of them, and EPL-Fin in particular turns out to be almost pure general factor with no domain-specific residual of its own. That is a coherent substantive story: questions about whether an estate can cover its debts, or whether a mortgaged house equals a cash account, draw on the same numeracy the FL items measure, while questions about what a power of attorney does draw on something more distinct.

For a write-up, the defensible pair of claims is: (a) EPL is empirically distinguishable from FL, which is H1 and is well supported; and (b) the three dimensions are nonetheless dominated by a common knowledge ability, so a total score is interpretable while subscale scores are not. “Closer to FL” remains a tendency in these data rather than a finding, and is a hypothesis for the next wave.

8 Summary Across All Specifications

Table 60. H1 and H2 in Both Samples
Sample N k items 1F CFI 2F CFI 3F CFI 3F RMSEA H1 p H1 supported H2 p H2 supported
Full 399 24 0.921 0.952 0.965 0.029 < .001 yes < .001 yes
Post-exclusion 372 24 0.915 0.950 0.966 0.026 < .001 yes < .001 yes

In both samples the two-factor model beats the one-factor model and the three-factor model beats the two-factor model. The estate planning literacy items are not simply additional indicators of general financial knowledge, and the financial-consequences and legal/administrative subscales are themselves separable. The exploratory analysis in Section 7 pushes this further: the three-factor structure also beats both alternative two-factor groupings, so “three constructs” is not an artifact of how the plan happened to draw the two-factor comparison.

Caveats that belong in any write-up of these results.

  • The latent factor correlations are high (FL–EPL r = 0.762; EPL-Fin–EPL-Legal r = 0.757). “Statistically distinguishable” is not “practically independent”; whether the distinction earns its keep is an incremental-validity question, which the plan reserves for exploratory work. The bifactor results in Section 7.5 sharpen this: a total score across all 24 items is well supported (ωH/ω = 0.85), but FL and EPL-Legal subscores are not (ωHS ≈ 0.29).
  • The EPL_FIN factor has only three indicators, which is the minimum for identification and gives the H2 comparison little room to be wrong in an interesting way. The bifactor analysis makes this concrete: those three items have no residual variance in common once a general factor is included, and the specific factor collapses entirely. A larger and more heterogeneous financial-consequences item pool would make H2 a much stronger test.
  • Scoring “I don’t know” as incorrect conflates not knowing with knowing-and-being-wrong. Given that EPL items draw far more blanks than FL items, some of the FL/EPL separation could reflect differing willingness to guess rather than differing knowledge. A supplementary model treating blanks as missing would speak to this, and is worth adding if a reviewer raises it.
  • fin_8 was dropped for non-discrimination rather than re-keyed, and should be retired from the FL scale in future waves. Dropping an item after inspecting it is a researcher degree of freedom; the justification and the numbers behind it are stated in the Summary so a reader can judge for themselves.
